The equilibrium constant depends on **temperature alone**.
Adding more H₂ and I₂ does disturb the system — Q falls below K, so the reaction shifts to
the left (towards HI) until Q equals K again — but the value of K itself does not move.
That is what makes K a constant: whatever the starting amounts, the equilibrium
concentrations always rearrange themselves so that the expression comes back to the same
number.
K = [H₂][I₂]/[HI]² = 6.4 before the addition, and 6.4 after it.
The temperature is unchanged at 300 K, so nothing can alter K.
Only a change in temperature alters K, because only then does ΔG° change, through
ΔG° = −RT ln K.
Adding a catalyst would not change it either — it would only make equilibrium arrive sooner.
∴ 6.4.
kcet|Chemistry|2009|16||0|0:
Physical adsorption is exothermic and reversible, so treat it as an equilibrium:
gas + surface ⇌ adsorbed gas + heat
Now apply Le Chatelier.
(4) Decreasing the temperature removes heat, so the system shifts to replace it — forward,
making more adsorption ✓
(2) Increasing the temperature does the opposite: the molecules gain enough energy to
overcome the weak van der Waals forces and desorb.
(1) Decreasing the pressure reduces the number of molecules striking the surface, so
adsorption falls. Raising it would increase adsorption.
(3) Decreasing the surface area leaves fewer sites, so less is adsorbed. This is why adsorbents
are used finely divided or porous — charcoal is activated precisely to maximise its area.
∴ a decrease in temperature.
kcet|Chemistry|2009|17||0|0:
The structure is (CH₃)₃C–Cl: a central carbon carrying three methyl groups and one chlorine.
Step 1 — find the longest chain **through** that carbon. Going from one methyl, through the
central carbon, to another methyl gives three carbons: propane.
Step 2 — number it. The central carbon is C2, and it carries the chlorine and the remaining
methyl as substituents.
Step 3 — name the substituents alphabetically: chloro before methyl.
That gives 2-chloro-2-methylpropane.
Option (2), t-butyl chloride, is the correct **common** name but not the IUPAC one, which is
what the question asks for.
Option (4) is wrong on two counts — the chain is propane not butane, and there is no position 3.
∴ 2-chloro-2-methylpropane.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|18||0|0.s:
The Lucas test distinguishes primary, secondary and tertiary **alcohols**.
The reagent is concentrated HCl with anhydrous ZnCl₂. It converts the alcohol to the alkyl
chloride, which is insoluble and appears as turbidity. How fast the cloudiness appears depends
on how easily a carbocation forms:
Tertiary alcohol — turbidity **immediately** (stable 3° carbocation)
Secondary alcohol — turbidity in about 5 minutes
Primary alcohol — no turbidity at room temperature; heating is needed
It is this graded response that makes the test useful.
Carboxylic acids are identified with sodium bicarbonate (effervescence), aldehydes with
Tollens' or Fehling's, and phenols with neutral FeCl₃ (violet colour) — each has its own test.
∴ alcohols.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|19||0|0:
Heating an organic compound with CuO is the standard combustion analysis: the CuO oxidises
the carbon to CO₂ and any hydrogen to H₂O.
So if CO₂ is produced, carbon is present ✓
If **no water** is produced, the compound contains **no hydrogen**.
Now check the options for a compound with carbon but no hydrogen:
(1) Methane, CH₄ — 4 hydrogens ✗
(2) Ethyl iodide, C₂H₅I — 5 hydrogens ✗
(4) Chloroform, CHCl₃ — one hydrogen, so a little water would form ✗
(3) Carbon tetrachloride, CCl₄ — carbon and chlorine only, no hydrogen at all ✓
Burning it gives CO₂ and chlorine-containing products, but not a trace of water.
Chloroform is the trap here: it looks hydrogen-free at a glance, but that single H would still
produce water.
∴ carbon tetrachloride.
kcet|Chemistry|2009|20||0|0:
A condensation polymer is formed by monomers joining with the **elimination of a small
molecule**, usually water. An addition polymer forms by monomers adding across a double
bond with nothing eliminated.
(1) PVC — addition polymer of vinyl chloride, CH₂=CHCl
(2) Polythene — addition polymer of ethene, CH₂=CH₂
(3) Rubber — addition polymer of isoprene
(4) Protein — amino acids condense through their –NH₂ and –COOH groups, losing one water
molecule at each link and forming a peptide (amide) bond ✓
n H₂N–CHR–COOH ⇒ [–NH–CHR–CO–]ₙ + (n − 1) H₂O
So protein is the only condensation polymer here. It is also a natural one; nylon and terylene
are the synthetic equivalents, joined by the same kind of condensation.
∴ protein.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|21||0|0.s:
The stability of a metal oxide is measured by how negative its free energy of formation is —
the basis of the Ellingham diagram. The more electropositive the metal, the greater its
affinity for oxygen and the more stable its oxide.
Rank the metals by electropositive character:
Mg > Al > Cr > Fe
So the oxides follow the same order of stability, with MgO the most stable and Fe₂O₃ the least.
Written as an **increasing** order:
Fe₂O₃ < Cr₂O₃ < Al₂O₃ < MgO
This ordering is the whole basis of metallurgical reduction: a metal will reduce the oxide of
any metal below it in the list. Aluminium reduces Fe₂O₃ and Cr₂O₃ — the thermite reaction —
but cannot reduce MgO, because magnesium's oxide is the more stable of the two.
∴ Fe₂O₃ < Cr₂O₃ < Al₂O₃ < MgO.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|22||0|0.s:
A blast furnace is hottest at the bottom, where the air blast burns the coke, and coolest at
the top. Working downwards:
Zone of reduction, 400–700 °C — CO reduces the iron oxides to spongy iron.
Zone of **slag formation**, 800–1000 °C — the limestone flux decomposes and the lime
combines with the silica gangue:
CaCO₃ ⇒ CaO + CO₂
CaO + SiO₂ ⇒ CaSiO₃ (slag)
Zone of fusion, 1200–1500 °C — the iron melts and absorbs carbon.
Zone of combustion, 1500–1600 °C — coke burns in the hot air blast, supplying the heat.
The slag zone is therefore the 800–1000 °C band, and the molten slag, being lighter, floats on
the iron below and is tapped off separately.
∴ 800–1000 °C.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|23||0|0.s:
In the contact process, sulphur dioxide is oxidised to the trioxide over a vanadium pentoxide
catalyst:
2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃
That catalyst is easily **poisoned**, and arsenic oxide, As₂O₃, carried along from the roasting
of sulphide ores, is the chief offender. It adsorbs onto the catalyst's active sites and blocks
them permanently.
So the gas has to be purified before it reaches the catalyst, and the arsenic is removed by
passing it through a purifying tower packed with freshly precipitated **ferric hydroxide**,
which adsorbs the As₂O₃.
The other purification steps use different units: a dust chamber for dust, a washing tower for
soluble impurities, and concentrated sulphuric acid in a drying tower for moisture.
∴ to remove arsenic impurity.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|24||0|0.s:
Check where ammonia is actually used as a reagent.
(1) Used ✓ — NH₄OH with NH₄Cl is the group reagent for group III basic radicals (Al³⁺, Fe³⁺,
Cr³⁺), precipitating them as hydroxides.
(2) Used ✓ — (NH₄)₂S in ammoniacal solution is the group reagent for group IV (Zn²⁺, Mn²⁺,
Co²⁺, Ni²⁺).
(3) Used ✓ — Tollens' reagent is ammoniacal silver nitrate, [Ag(NH₃)₂]OH; the ammonia is
essential, since it dissolves the silver oxide as the diammine complex.
(4) **Not** used — Nessler's reagent is an alkaline solution of potassium tetraiodomercurate(II),
K₂[HgI₄] in KOH. There is no ammonia in it.
The confusion is understandable: Nessler's reagent is the reagent used to **detect** ammonia,
giving a brown precipitate. It is the thing ammonia is tested *with*, not a thing made *from* it.
∴ ammonia is not used in Nessler's reagent.
